extracted.intended_audience: research software authors, JOSS editors, and volunteer reviewers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and review checklist for submitting, reviewing, and accepting short software-describing articles to the Journal of Open Source Software (JOSS). Covers submission eligibility, required software/artifact characteristics, and the reviewer checklist used during open GitHub reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open-source license requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The software must be open source by the Open Source Initiative (OSI) definition (open-source.org).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repository must contain a plain-text LICENSE file with the contents of an OSI-approved software license (see opensource.org/licenses/alphabetical). This is a hard eligibility requirement for JOSS submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research application
rubrics_metrics.description: The software must have a research application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: JOSS only accepts software that is intended to be used for research; domain research results belong in domain journals, not in JOSS.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submitter contribution / authorship eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The submitter should be a major contributor to the software they are submitting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers/editors check that the submitting author actually made major contributions; authorship decisions otherwise are left to the project but may be discussed with reviewers/editors if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Significance / novelty of contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: The software should be a significant new contribution to the available open-source software that either enables some new research challenge(s) or makes addressing research challenges significantly better (e.g., faster, easier, simpler).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: JOSS expects submissions to be more than trivial wrappers or incremental, incomplete pieces; the software should materially help research workflows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feature-complete requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The software should be feature-complete, i.e., it cannot be a partial solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partial prototypes or incomplete, non-functional code bases are not acceptable; the package should be in a state where its core functionality can be evaluated and used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article format and content limits
rubrics_metrics.description: JOSS articles are deliberately short and only include an abstract describing the high-level functionality of the software, a list of the authors (with affiliations), key references, and a link to the software archive and repository.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Articles must not include API descriptions or domain research results; the software API should be documented in the software's own documentation and research results should be published in domain journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Software archival requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors must archive the software (including changes made during review) with a service such as Zenodo or Figshare and post a link (DOI) to the archive in the review thread.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The archival DOI is associated with the submission (commanded into the review by the editor/bot) and is required before final acceptance/publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Article and code licensing (publication-level)
rubrics_metrics.description: Submitting authors retain copyright of their JOSS article, which is published under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License; any code snippets included in JOSS articles are subject to the MIT license regardless of the submitted software's license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure compliance with CC-BY 4.0 for the article text and MIT for inline code snippets; submitted software itself must use an OSI-approved license.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review focus on software artifacts
rubrics_metrics.description: JOSS peer review targets the software components: functionality, documentation, tests, continuous integration, and the license.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers are expected to examine the repository contents (code, tests, docs, CI configuration) and not only the short article text. The review checklist was based on rOpenSci onboarding practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict of interest declaration (reviewer)
rubrics_metrics.description: As the reviewer I confirm that I have read the JOSS conflict of interest policy and that there are no conflicts of interest for me to review this work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers must proactively check for and declare COI before proceeding; this is part of the required checklist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Code of Conduct adherence (reviewer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers must confirm that they have read and will adhere to the JOSS code of conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All interactions in the open GitHub review thread must follow the JOSS Code of Conduct (adopted from the Contributor Covenant). Authors also confirm adherence during submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repository availability check
rubrics_metrics.description: Repository: Is the source code for this software available at the repository URL?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer should verify that the provided repository URL points to the actual source code; discoverability and correct repository linking are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: License file presence and correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: License: Does the repository contain a plain-text LICENSE file with the contents of an OSI-approved software license?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer must ensure the license file exists, is machine-readable (plain-text), and is one of the OSI-approved licenses; lack of proper license blocks acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Release version consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Version: Does the release version given match the GitHub release?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check that the version referenced in the paper/metadata corresponds to an actual release/tag in the repository and to the archived DOI.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship verification (general checks)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorship: Has the submitting author made major contributions to the software?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This repeats the submission eligibility check; reviewers should look at contribution history, commit authorship, or project documentation to confirm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Installation verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Installation: Does installation proceed as outlined in the documentation?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer should attempt installation following documented steps, verify dependency specifications, and note issues; recommend use of automated package management when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional claims verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Functionality: Have the functional claims of the software been confirmed?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer should exercise core features or run provided examples to confirm that the software performs as the authors claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance claims verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Performance: Have any performance claims of the software been confirmed?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If authors claim particular performance characteristics (speed, scalability), reviewers should validate these claims where feasible or note inability to reproduce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statement of need (documentation)
rubrics_metrics.description: A statement of need: Do the authors clearly state what problems the software is designed to solve and who the target audience is?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This appears both as a documentation requirement and as part of the short paper; clarity about purpose and audience is essential for acceptance and for users to judge suitability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Installation instructions and dependency specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Installation instructions: Is there a clearly-stated list of dependencies? Ideally these should be handled with an automated package management solution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dependencies should be explicit, pinned where appropriate, and ideally installable through standard package managers or environment specifications (e.g., requirements.txt, environment.yml, DESCRIPTION).

rubrics_metrics.name: Example usage and real-world examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Example usage: Do the authors include examples of how to use the software (ideally to solve real-world analysis problems)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Useful examples make it easier for reviewers and users to validate functionality; examples should be runnable and representative of typical use-cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functionality documentation / API docs
rubrics_metrics.description: Functionality documentation: Is the core functionality of the software documented to a satisfactory level (e.g., API method documentation)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: API reference, readme explanations, and higher-level user guides should make core functions discoverable and usable by target audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Automated tests or verification steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Automated tests: Are there automated tests or manual steps described so that the function of the software can be verified?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presence of test suites (unit/integration) and instructions to run them is strongly encouraged; reviewers should run tests when possible and report failures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community and contribution guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Community guidelines: Are there clear guidelines for third parties wishing to (1) contribute to the software, (2) report issues or problems with the software, and (3) seek support?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CONTRIBUTING, ISSUE_TEMPLATE, and SUPPORT or README sections should clearly state how to contribute, report bugs, or request help; these foster future maintenance and community uptake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Software paper metadata checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors: Does the paper.md file include a list of authors with their affiliations?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The short paper must list authors and affiliations to support indexing and credit; editors use this to populate Crossref metadata.

rubrics_metrics.name: Software paper: statement of need and references
rubrics_metrics.description: Software paper: A statement of need and References: Do the authors clearly state the problem solved and do all archival references that should have a DOI list one (e.g., papers, datasets, software)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References should include DOIs where available to facilitate indexing and proper credit; the short paper duplicates the repository's statement of need at a high level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open/public peer review and transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: JOSS conducts open peer review on GitHub: reviews occur in public GitHub issues where editors, reviewers, and authors discuss issues openly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The review process is collaborative and transparent; reviewers and authors should exchange comments publicly and adhere to the code of conduct. This transparency also allows community members to volunteer or contribute feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fast-track for rOpenSci-reviewed submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: For submissions of software already reviewed under rOpenSci’s onboarding guidelines, JOSS does not perform further review and may fast-track acceptance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A note linking to the rOpenSci onboarding issue is added and the editor-in-chief is alerted; this avoids duplication of review effort for rigorously reviewed rOpenSci packages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational metadata and DOI deposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Once accepted, JOSS gives the article a DOI, deposits metadata in Crossref, and updates the JOSS website and review thread with DOI and status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors (currently via Whedon / Whedon-API) compile the article, prepare Crossref metadata, and perform final acceptance steps; authors should ensure metadata in the submission form and paper.md is correct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance policy regarding major revisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlike other journals, JOSS does not reject articles requiring major revision; while not yet accepted, articles remain visible and under review until the authors make adequate changes (or withdraw).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The default disposition is to work with authors to improve the software/package until it meets criteria rather than issuing rejections after major revisions are requested.
